item.text:
Rain begins with water that is already moving through the environment. Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes. On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. Thunderstorms can produce heavy showers when strong rising currents carry warm, moist air high into the atmosphere. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Rain is part of a continuing cycle. Water that reaches the ground may flow into streams and rivers, soak into soil, fill lakes, or seep underground. Some is taken up by plants, and some evaporates back into the air. Eventually, water vapor may rise, cool, condense, and form clouds again.

The basic ingredients are moisture, cooling, and a way to make cloud particles grow. Sunlight helps supply the moisture by driving evaporation; rising air commonly provides the cooling; and collisions or ice growth help form drops large enough to fall. The details vary from one cloud and weather system to another, but rain forms whenever the atmosphere gathers water, cools it into cloud particles, and grows those particles until gravity brings them down.

Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

Rain begins with water that is already moving through the environment. Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice.

As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

Rain begins with water that is already moving through the environment. Sunlight warms oceans, lakes, rivers, and damp ground. Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes.

As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Together, these processes add moisture to the air.

Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes. On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. Thunderstorms can produce heavy showers when strong rising currents carry warm, moist air high into the atmosphere. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes. On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. Thunderstorms can produce heavy showers when strong rising currents carry warm, moist air high into the atmosphere. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Some of this water changes from liquid into an invisible gas called water vapor. Plants also release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves. Warm air can hold more water vapor than cool air. When the air near the ground warms, it often rises. It may rise because the ground has heated it, because wind pushes it up a hillside, or because two large bodies of air meet and one is forced over the other. As the air rises, the air pressure around it decreases. The rising air expands, and expansion makes it cool.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes. On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. Thunderstorms can produce heavy showers when strong rising currents carry warm, moist air high into the atmosphere. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Rain is part of a continuing cycle. Water that reaches the ground may flow into streams and rivers, soak into soil, fill lakes, or seep underground. Some is taken up by plants, and some evaporates back into the air. Eventually, water vapor may rise, cool, condense, and form clouds again.

Cooling is important because air has a limit to how much water vapor it can contain. If moist air cools enough, it reaches that limit. Scientists call this point the dew point. Beyond it, the air cannot keep all its water as vapor. Some of the vapor changes back into liquid water, a process called condensation.

Condensation usually happens around tiny particles floating in the air, such as dust, sea salt, smoke, or pollen. These particles provide surfaces on which water can gather. Each begins as an extremely small droplet. The droplets make clouds visible: a cloud is a vast collection of tiny water droplets, ice crystals, or both, suspended in the air.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.

Not every cloud produces rain. Cloud droplets are so small that air currents can keep them aloft. A droplet may be only a fraction of a millimeter across, far too light to fall quickly. For rain to form, droplets must grow large and heavy enough to overcome the upward motion of the air.

In warm clouds, droplets grow mainly through collisions. They move at different speeds and along slightly different paths. Larger droplets tend to fall faster than smaller ones, bumping into them as they descend. If the droplets stick together, they combine into bigger drops. This repeated process can produce raindrops large enough to fall from the cloud. A raindrop’s familiar shape is not a tiny teardrop: small drops are nearly spherical, while larger ones flatten at the bottom as air pushes against them.

In colder clouds, the process often involves ice. A cloud may contain both supercooled liquid droplets, which remain liquid below freezing, and ice crystals. Water vapor can deposit onto the ice crystals, and the crystals grow. They may also collect supercooled droplets that freeze on contact. As the crystals become heavier, they fall and may join with other crystals to form snowflakes or other ice particles.

What happens next depends on the temperatures between the cloud and the ground. If the air stays cold, the ice can reach the surface as snow or another form of frozen precipitation. If the ice falls through a warm layer, it melts and becomes rain. Sometimes a deep layer of cold air near the ground freezes falling rain into ice pellets. In other situations, liquid drops become supercooled in the air and freeze when they touch cold surfaces, creating freezing rain.

A raindrop also has to survive the journey down. In dry air, some water evaporates before it reaches the ground. This can make rain fade away beneath a cloud, leaving the surface dry. If the air below the cloud is moist enough, more of the falling water reaches the ground. Winds can move the drops sideways, so rain may fall some distance from the place where the air first rose or the cloud first formed.

The shape and movement of clouds influence where rain falls. Hills and mountains lift air and can encourage clouds to form on their windward slopes. On the other side, descending air often warms and dries, so that area may receive less rain. Large weather systems can lift air over broad regions, producing steady precipitation. Thunderstorms can produce heavy showers when strong rising currents carry warm, moist air high into the atmosphere. As the cloud grows, falling water and ice can strengthen the currents and contribute to sudden, intense rain.
